m: A normal first ECG rules out acute coronary syndrome.
fix: Up to half of early ECGs are non-diagnostic; repeat ECGs and serial troponins are needed before ruling it out.

m: Troponin rises within minutes of myocardial injury, so a single early value is enough.
fix: Troponin takes about 3–6 hours to rise with conventional assays; serial testing is needed, and it also rises in non-ischaemic injury.

m: Heart failure always means a low ejection fraction.
fix: About half of patients have preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), with diastolic dysfunction as the main problem.

m: Hypertension causes headache, so a patient without symptoms is unlikely to be hypertensive.
fix: Hypertension is usually asymptomatic until organ damage occurs; it is detected by measurement, not symptoms.

m: Blood pressure in a hypertensive emergency should be brought to normal as fast as possible.
fix: Lower mean arterial pressure by no more than about 25% in the first hour; rapid normalisation risks cerebral, coronary and renal ischaemia.

m: The loudness of a murmur reflects the severity of the valve lesion.
fix: Loudness correlates poorly with severity; in severe aortic stenosis the murmur may soften as cardiac output falls.

m: The aortic valve is the valve most commonly affected in rheumatic heart disease.
fix: The mitral valve is most commonly involved, followed by the aortic valve.

m: A negative single blood culture excludes infective endocarditis.
fix: At least three sets from separate sites are needed before antibiotics; culture-negative endocarditis also exists.

m: All hyponatraemia should be treated with normal saline.
fix: Treatment depends on volume status: saline for hypovolaemia but fluid restriction for SIADH; correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.

m: Calcium gluconate lowers serum potassium in hyperkalaemia.
fix: Calcium only stabilises the cardiac membrane; insulin-glucose and beta-agonists shift potassium into cells, and binders or dialysis remove it.

m: Potassium replacement will correct hypokalaemia even if magnesium is low.
fix: Hypomagnesaemia causes ongoing renal potassium loss; magnesium must be corrected for potassium to normalise.

m: Most hypercalcaemia in hospital patients is due to primary hyperparathyroidism.
fix: Primary hyperparathyroidism is commonest in outpatients; malignancy is the leading cause in hospitalised patients.

m: A conscious patient with hypoglycaemia needs intravenous dextrose.
fix: If the patient can swallow, oral fast-acting glucose is first-line; IV dextrose or glucagon is for those who cannot.

m: In diabetic ketoacidosis insulin should be started before checking potassium.
fix: Check potassium first; insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause dangerous hypokalaemia if it is already low.

m: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is just a milder form of diabetic ketoacidosis.
fix: It has higher mortality, marked dehydration and hyperosmolality with little ketosis, and needs slower, fluid-led correction.

m: Type 2 diabetes never needs insulin.
fix: Many patients need insulin as beta-cell function declines, or during illness, surgery or pregnancy.

m: A normal TSH excludes all thyroid disease.
fix: TSH can be misleading in pituitary disease, recent treatment change and non-thyroidal illness; free T4 is needed in those settings.

m: A normal early CT scan rules out ischaemic stroke.
fix: Early CT is often normal in ischaemic stroke; its main early role is to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis.

m: A sudden severe headache that settles with analgesics is unlikely to be serious.
fix: Thunderclap headache needs evaluation for subarachnoid haemorrhage regardless of response to analgesia.

m: Sepsis requires a fever.
fix: Older, immunosuppressed and very ill patients may be normothermic or hypothermic; hypothermia is a poor prognostic sign.

m: Melaena always means bleeding from the upper GI tract.
fix: Melaena usually indicates a source proximal to the ligament of Treitz, but small-bowel or right-colon bleeding with slow transit can also cause it.

m: Normal transaminases exclude significant liver disease.
fix: Transaminases may be normal in compensated cirrhosis; synthetic function (albumin, INR) and imaging matter more.

m: An exudate is diagnosed only by high pleural protein.
fix: Light's criteria use protein and LDH ratios and pleural LDH; any one criterion classifies the fluid as an exudate.

m: Adding a single new drug to a failing TB regimen is a reasonable step.
fix: Adding one drug to a failing regimen promotes further resistance; regimens are changed on the basis of drug-susceptibility testing.

m: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis can be skipped if the animal looks healthy.
fix: Category II–III exposures need prophylaxis started immediately; observation of a dog or cat can only stop it later.

m: A tourniquet and incision help a snakebite victim.
fix: Tourniquets, incision and suction are harmful; immobilise the limb and transfer for antivenom.

m: Delirium in older adults is usually hyperactive and obvious.
fix: Hypoactive delirium is common and easily missed as depression or tiredness; screen actively.

m: Memory loss in older people is a normal part of ageing.
fix: Progressive memory loss that affects daily function is not normal ageing and needs evaluation for dementia and reversible causes.

m: All anaemia in women is iron deficiency and can be treated with iron without tests.
fix: Red cell indices and iron studies are needed; thalassaemia trait and B12 or folate deficiency need different management.

m: A normal serum ferritin excludes iron deficiency in an inflamed patient.
fix: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; it may be normal or high despite iron deficiency in inflammation.

m: Folic acid alone is safe treatment for any macrocytic anaemia.
fix: Folate alone in B12 deficiency can worsen neurological damage; check and replace B12 first.

m: Thalassaemia trait needs iron supplements because the cells are microcytic.
fix: Iron stores are normal in trait; unnecessary iron risks overload. Distinguish it from iron deficiency with iron studies and HbA2.

m: Sickle cell trait carriers commonly have painful crises.
fix: Trait is usually asymptomatic; crises occur in homozygous sickle cell disease.

m: DIC is only a bleeding disorder.
fix: DIC involves widespread microthrombi and consumption of factors and platelets; organ damage from thrombosis is common.

m: Every child with immune thrombocytopenia needs platelet transfusion.
fix: Most childhood ITP resolves spontaneously; transfusion is for life-threatening bleeding only, because platelets are rapidly destroyed.

m: A normal white cell count excludes leukaemia.
fix: Leukaemia can present with a low or normal count; the blood film and bone marrow are diagnostic.

m: Myeloma lesions are reliably detected by a bone scan.
fix: Lytic myeloma lesions often do not show on isotope bone scan; a skeletal survey, CT or MRI is used.

m: Painful lymph nodes are typical of lymphoma.
fix: Lymphoma nodes are typically painless and rubbery; pain is more typical of infection (alcohol-induced pain is a rare exception).

m: Nephrotic syndrome causes visible blood in the urine.
fix: Nephrotic syndrome features heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; haematuria and hypertension point to nephritic syndrome.

m: Serum creatinine rises immediately after kidney injury.
fix: Creatinine lags behind injury by 24–48 hours; urine output and trends matter early.

m: Small kidneys are required to diagnose chronic kidney disease.
fix: Kidneys may be normal-sized or large in diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis and polycystic disease.

m: All kidney stones are visible on plain X-ray.
fix: Uric acid stones are radiolucent; non-contrast CT is the most sensitive test.

m: Cirrhosis is caused only by alcohol.
fix: Viral hepatitis B and C, fatty liver disease, autoimmune and metabolic diseases are major causes.

m: Hepatitis A commonly becomes chronic.
fix: Hepatitis A and E do not usually cause chronic infection; hepatitis B and C do.

m: The height of serum amylase or lipase indicates the severity of pancreatitis.
fix: Enzyme levels support diagnosis but do not predict severity; clinical scores and organ failure do.

m: Appendicitis always starts with pain in the right iliac fossa.
fix: Pain classically starts periumbilical and migrates; retrocaecal and pelvic positions and pregnancy change the picture.

m: Stress and spicy food are the main causes of peptic ulcers.
fix: Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes.

m: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis both affect only the colon.
fix: Crohn disease can affect any part of the GI tract with skip lesions; ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum.

m: Rectal bleeding in an older adult can be attributed to haemorrhoids without further tests.
fix: New rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habit in older adults needs evaluation for colorectal cancer.

m: Wheeze is always present in a severe asthma attack.
fix: A silent chest signals life-threatening asthma with minimal air movement.

m: Oxygen should be given to reach 100% saturation in COPD exacerbation.
fix: In patients at risk of hypercapnia, target saturations of about 88–92% to avoid worsening CO2 retention.

m: A normal chest examination rules out pneumonia.
fix: Examination is insensitive; a chest X-ray is needed when pneumonia is suspected.

m: A negative sputum smear excludes pulmonary tuberculosis.
fix: Smear has limited sensitivity; nucleic acid amplification tests (e.g. CBNAAT) and culture are more sensitive.

m: Lung cancer occurs only in smokers.
fix: Smoking is the main risk, but adenocarcinoma occurs in never-smokers, and occupational exposures also contribute.

m: Bronchiectasis is diagnosed reliably on chest X-ray.
fix: High-resolution CT is the diagnostic test; plain films are often normal or non-specific.

m: Lumbar puncture must always be done before antibiotics in suspected meningitis.
fix: Antibiotics should not be delayed; if LP is delayed (e.g. for CT), take blood cultures and give antibiotics first.

m: A single negative smear rules out malaria.
fix: Repeat smears or rapid tests at intervals are needed when clinical suspicion persists.

m: The Widal test in the first week reliably confirms typhoid.
fix: Blood culture is the test of choice in the first week; Widal has poor sensitivity and specificity, especially in endemic areas.

m: A positive ANA test confirms lupus.
fix: ANA is sensitive but not specific; healthy people can be positive. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are more specific.

m: A negative rheumatoid factor excludes rheumatoid arthritis.
fix: Up to a third of patients are seronegative; anti-CCP is more specific and diagnosis is clinical.

m: A normal serum uric acid during an attack excludes gout.
fix: Uric acid can be normal during an acute attack; joint aspiration showing urate crystals is diagnostic.

m: Osteoarthritis is an inflammatory arthritis with prolonged morning stiffness.
fix: Osteoarthritis is degenerative, with brief (<30 min) stiffness; prolonged stiffness suggests inflammatory arthritis.

m: All thyrotoxicosis is Graves disease and needs antithyroid drugs.
fix: Thyroiditis causes transient thyrotoxicosis from release of stored hormone; antithyroid drugs do not help it.

m: Thyroxine should be started at full dose in all patients.
fix: Older adults and those with heart disease start low and titrate slowly to avoid precipitating ischaemia.

m: The commonest cause of Cushing syndrome is a pituitary adenoma.
fix: Exogenous glucocorticoid use is the commonest cause; Cushing disease is the commonest endogenous cause.

m: Steroids can be stopped suddenly after long-term use.
fix: Long-term steroids suppress the axis; abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis, so taper.

m: A painless breast lump is less worrying than a painful one.
fix: Most breast cancers are painless; any new lump needs triple assessment.

m: A normal PSA excludes prostate cancer.
fix: PSA has limited sensitivity and specificity; examination and further tests are needed when suspicion exists.

m: Cervical cancer screening is only needed after symptoms appear.
fix: Screening detects pre-invasive disease in asymptomatic women; HPV infection is the necessary cause.

m: Carcinomas mainly spread through the blood and sarcomas through lymphatics.
fix: Carcinomas typically spread first by lymphatics and sarcomas by blood (with exceptions such as RCC, HCC, follicular thyroid).

m: Apoptosis and necrosis both cause inflammation.
fix: Necrosis provokes inflammation; apoptosis is programmed cell death with intact membranes and little inflammation.

m: Dysplasia is the same as cancer.
fix: Dysplasia is disordered growth that may regress; it becomes invasive cancer only after the basement membrane is breached.

m: Anaphylaxis is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
fix: Anaphylaxis is a type I IgE-mediated immediate reaction; type IV is delayed and T-cell mediated.

m: Pulmonary embolism always causes chest pain and haemoptysis.
fix: Unexplained breathlessness and tachycardia are the commonest features; the classic triad is often absent.

m: A normal D-dimer excludes DVT in any patient.
fix: D-dimer only helps exclude DVT when pre-test probability is low; high-probability patients need imaging.

m: Amyloid is a single protein that causes one disease.
fix: Amyloid is a misfolded beta-pleated structure formed by different proteins (AL, AA, ATTR), each with different causes.

m: Antibiotics treat COVID-19 pneumonia.
fix: COVID-19 is viral; antibiotics are for documented or strongly suspected bacterial co-infection only.

m: Leprosy is highly contagious through brief skin contact.
fix: Transmission needs prolonged close contact, mainly via nasal droplets; most people are naturally resistant and treated patients are non-infectious.

m: Paraneoplastic syndromes are caused by direct spread of the tumour.
fix: They are caused by hormones, cytokines or antibodies produced by or against the tumour, at sites remote from it.

m: Normal blood pressure excludes shock.
fix: Compensated shock maintains BP; tachycardia, raised lactate, poor perfusion and low urine output appear first.

m: Jaundice with dark urine means haemolysis.
fix: Dark urine reflects conjugated bilirubin (hepatic or obstructive); haemolytic jaundice is acholuric.

m: Cyanosis is a reliable sign of hypoxia in anaemic patients.
fix: Cyanosis needs about 5 g/dL of deoxygenated haemoglobin, so severe anaemia can mask hypoxia.

m: Syncope with jerking movements is always a seizure.
fix: Brief myoclonic jerks are common in syncope; rapid recovery without prolonged confusion favours syncope.

m: Fever should always be suppressed with antipyretics.
fix: Antipyretics are for comfort; the cause matters more, and fever height does not reliably indicate severity.

m: All oedema should be treated with diuretics.
fix: Treat the cause; diuretics may harm in hypovolaemia, and lymphoedema or venous oedema responds poorly.

m: Loss of sensation and loss of power always occur together after nerve injury.
fix: Pure motor, pure sensory or mixed deficits depend on the nerve and level injured.

m: Weakness in myasthenia gravis is worst in the morning.
fix: Weakness worsens with activity and later in the day (fatigability).

c: Upper and lower motor neuron lesions
m: Acute upper motor neuron lesions always cause spasticity and brisk reflexes.
fix: In the acute phase (spinal or cerebral shock) tone and reflexes may be reduced before UMN signs appear.
